title: Outbound network: egress, allowlists and static IP
standfirst: What the agent can reach, what can be blocked, and whether the outside world sees a stable address. This is where an agent that browses meets a firewall that was designed for a web app.
idea: Outbound access is usually open by default, because an agent that cannot reach a package registry is not much use. The interesting parts are the controls: can you deny everything, allow a list of hosts, and enforce it outside the machine so root inside cannot loosen it?

A static egress IP is a separate product. It matters when a third-party API allowlists your address, or when a rate limit is shared with every other sandbox on the host. Most providers here do not offer one; Runtime sells it for $5 a month, and E2B explicitly does not offer it on any plan.

The last question is billing. Egress is free at some providers, metered at others, and unpublished at a few. A generous free allowance can be the difference between a cheap agent and an expensive one.

splits.heading: Open by default, closed on request
body: Runtime starts closed and makes you open a door; a sandbox can also be set to `internet: false` or an allowlist. Agent 37 offers allow-all, deny-all and an IPv4 allowlist, changeable live, and DNS counts as a connection. boxd's allowlist is enforced outside the machine, so root cannot loosen it.

Sandboxer, Lizard, InstaBox and Boat are open by default with no published allowlist. Boat has no API setting for network rules at all; its firewall is ufw inside the sandbox, and rules do not survive a snapshot.

splits.heading: A stable address is rare
body: Runtime sells a dedicated outbound address per account for $5 a month. Vercel's Secure Compute gives a private path to AWS, but the public path is billed as data transfer. Most others share an address: Sandboxer says outbound traffic shares the node's IP, and InstaBox's machines share one NAT address according to a third party.

E2B is explicit that there are no dedicated or static egress IPs on any plan, including Enterprise. A customer-operated proxy is the documented workaround. Morph charges egress as a billing component but publishes no rate, allowlist or static address.

splits.heading: Filtering is not the same as blocking
body: Blaxel's proxy can filter domains, but traffic from tools that ignore proxy environment variables is not filtered unless domain filter enforcement is enabled. Vercel's firewall matchers select requests for transformation and never block a request by themselves.
That distinction matters for an agent that runs arbitrary binaries: a proxy that only sees well-behaved HTTP clients is not a network boundary.

watchFor: Whether the default is open or closed, and whether a deny-all rule also blocks DNS.
Whether the allowlist is enforced outside the machine, or by a proxy the agent can bypass.
Whether there is a static egress IP, and what it costs.
Whether egress is free, metered, or unpublished.
Whether sandboxes can reach each other over a private network.

rows.scenario: The agent's package downloads go out through the allowlist, and no egress rate or cap is published to price them.
rows.note: Allow-all, deny-all or an IPv4 allowlist of up to 100 entries, changeable live. DNS counts as a connection, and private ranges stay blocked. No static egress IP or published egress price.

source.quote: **DNS counts as a connection.** Under `deny-all` or a list, names do not resolve unless a resolver is on the list.

rows.scenario: Egress is included, and the proxy can filter domains, but tools that ignore proxy variables are not filtered unless enforcement is on.
rows.note: A proxy can filter domains, but tools that ignore proxy environment variables are not filtered unless domain filter enforcement is enabled. Egress is included in the plan.

rows.scenario: Nothing is billed for traffic, and there is no API for network rules; ufw inside the sandbox is the control.
rows.note: Outbound is open by default with no API for network rules; ufw inside the sandbox is the control, and firewall rules do not survive a snapshot. Egress is not billed.

source.quote: Network traffic. boat does not bill egress.

rows.scenario: The allowlist is enforced outside the machine, so root inside cannot loosen it, and no egress price is published.
rows.note: A per-machine allowlist enforced outside the machine, so root inside cannot loosen it. Forks inherit it; a machine from a snapshot starts unrestricted.

source.quote: An allowlist of just `none` cuts the machine off from the internet entirely.

rows.scenario: Outbound is off unless `enableInternet` is true; with it off, only allowedHosts or an outbound handler on ports 80 and 443 can leave.
rows.note: Off by default; only ports 80 and 443 through allowedHosts or an outbound handler. No static egress IP or private network. 1 TB a month is included in North America and Europe, then $0.025/GB; 500 GB elsewhere, then $0.04–$0.05.

source.quote: A Container starts with `enableInternet: false` by default, so it cannot reach the Internet.

rows.scenario: Package installs fail on Tier 1: outbound is restricted and cannot be overridden per sandbox; full internet needs a $500 top-up.
rows.note: Tier 1 and 2 are restricted and cannot be overridden per sandbox; Tier 3 and 4 get full internet. Per-sandbox controls are block-all, CIDR, domain or an upstream proxy. No static egress IP or egress price is published.

source.quote: **Tier 1 & Tier 2**: Network access is restricted and cannot be overridden at the sandbox level.

rows.scenario: Domain and IP allow and deny rules are documented, but there is no dedicated egress address on any plan.
rows.note: Outbound is open by default with documented domain and IP allow and deny rules. No dedicated or static egress IP on any plan, including Enterprise.

source.quote: there are no dedicated or static egress IP addresses on any plan (including Enterprise).

rows.scenario: Each plan includes outbound data every month (100 GiB on Free, 1 TiB on Pro), then $0.02 per GiB. InstaBox's docs say nothing about which address outbound traffic leaves from.
rows.note: No general egress allowlist is published; host scoping applies to Secrets, not all sandbox traffic. Each plan includes egress every month (100 GiB Free, 1 TiB Pro, 5 TiB Builder, 50 TiB Team), then $0.02 per GiB. Outbound addresses are not published.

rows.scenario: No per-GB charge inside 2 TB per account over a rolling 30 days, with no documented allowlist.
rows.note: Outbound is open with no documented allowlist. Sandbox egress has no per-GB charge, with 2 TB per account over a rolling 30 days included.

source.quote: Sandbox egress has no separate per-GB charge. The included allowance is 2 TB per account over a rolling 30 days

rows.scenario: The download runs on the open default; over the plan allowance it bills $0.04 a GiB, including private traffic between containers.
rows.note: Open by default, with block-all, CIDR and domain allowlists; DNS leaks past the allowlists. Static IPs come from Proxies on Team and Enterprise. Egress is $0.04/GiB over 1, 10 or 100 TiB by plan.

source.quote: By default, Sandboxes can make outbound connections to any public IP address.

rows.scenario: Egress is a chargeable component in the terms, with no published rate, allowlist or static address.
rows.note: Egress is a chargeable component in the terms, but no per-GB rate, allowlist, static IP or filtering is published. Do not assume egress is free.

source.quote: Typical components may include but are not limited to compute, snapshot storage, and egress.

rows.scenario: A dedicated outbound address costs $5 a month; without it the sandbox can be set to refuse everything or to an allowlist.
rows.note: `internet: false` refuses everything, an allow list is allow-list only, and deny always wins. A dedicated outbound address costs $5 a month, and sandboxes reach each other over a private name.

source.quote: Dedicated IPv4 | $5 | per 30-day month

rows.scenario: Outbound is open with no allowlist, and traffic shares the node's IPv4 with other sandboxes.
rows.note: Outbound is open by default with no allowlist product. Traffic shares the node's IPv4 and IPv6 with other sandboxes, so external rate limits are shared.

source.quote: outbound internet is open by default

rows.scenario: Outbound is unrestricted, bandwidth is not metered, and a DNS allowlist is opt-in and applied from outside.
rows.note: Outbound is unrestricted by default, with an opt-in DNS allowlist applied from outside the Sprite. Bandwidth is not metered.

source.quote: Applying one is opt-in and done from outside the Sprite.

rows.scenario: Firewall rules default to allow-all, and traffic beyond the included 20 GB a month bills at $0.15 per GB.
rows.note: Firewall rules default to allow-all and can be set per sandbox. Matchers transform requests but never block them, so an allowlist needs an explicit rule.

source.quote: Sandbox Data Transfer | 20 GB/month | Included in Flat Rate CDN | $0.15/GB

rows.scenario: Egress is open by default and can be turned into an allowlist or a denylist, replaced live on a running sandbox; the traffic itself is not billed.
rows.note: `allow_out` takes domains, leading-wildcard domains, IPv4 addresses and CIDRs; `deny_out` wins on a conflict. The policy can be swapped on a running sandbox as one atomic change that closes existing connections, and a hostname that will not resolve rejects the update. `allow_internet_access=false` with an empty allowlist blocks DNS too. Egress is free.

source.quote: values can be domains, leading-wildcard domains like `*.example.com`, IPv4 addresses, or IPv4 CIDR ranges

rows.scenario: Outbound data is included per plan, 500 GiB to 11,000 GiB pooled across the team, then $0.01 a GiB.
rows.note: Allowances are pooled at team level with no rollover. Cloud firewalls filter by protocol, port and address in both directions at no extra cost. Each Droplet keeps its public IPv4 for its life, and Reserved IPs give a movable inbound address.

source.quote: Each Droplet plan includes an amount of free outbound data transfer. Additional outbound transfer is billed at $0.01 per GiB.

rows.scenario: The agent browses freely inside a 20 TB EU allowance from a static IPv4, and outbound rules can restrict where it goes.
rows.note: Each server includes 20 TB of outbound traffic in the EU (1 TB in the US, 0.5 TB in Singapore) with overage at €1.00/$1.20 per TB, incoming and internal traffic free. Cloud Firewalls filter outgoing traffic as well as incoming and are free, and a server can be created with no public IP at all.

source.quote: A Firewall is used to restrict the incoming and outgoing traffic a user wants on the server.

rows.scenario: The 400 GB download fits inside KVM 2's 8 TB; after the allowance the link drops to 10 Mbps, not a bill.
rows.note: 4 TB on KVM 1 up to 32 TB on KVM 8, with no per-GiB overage charge; exceeding the allowance throttles to 10 Mbps until the next month. A dedicated IPv4 gives a stable outgoing address, though the terms allow a change on migration. The managed firewall filters incoming traffic only, so there is no provider-level outbound allowlist or no-internet mode.

source.quote: 4 TB bandwidth

rows.scenario: Call the API: outbound is denied until a firewall rule allows it, and the first 50 GB (Free) or 500 GB (paid) of transfer is included.
rows.note: Allowlist by domain, CIDR or identity. Default deny, so no internet until a rule allows it. Every VM shares one account-level outbound IPv4, but Freestyle does not promise it stays fixed.

source.quote: A VM gets nothing implicitly — no outbound Internet, no inbound

rows.scenario: Outbound data is included up to the plan's monthly cap, and running past it stops the server rather than billing overage.
rows.note: Each plan includes 1–32 TB a month with inbound and outbound counted together; extra capacity is 10 SEK per TB a month, up to 500 TB. There is no metered overage: when the allowance is gone the server cannot start until you buy more or the period resets. The panel firewall is inbound only, so there is no egress allowlist and no way to switch the internet off. The address is stable — HostUp owns its RIPE subnets and the IP stays with the server.

source.quote: If the bandwidth runs out, the server cannot be started or restarted until you buy more or the next period starts.

rows.scenario: The agent browses freely from a static IPv4 with no per-GiB bill, but restricting where it can go means iptables or ufw inside the guest, which a root agent can change.
rows.note: Unlimited traffic at 500 Mbps to 3 Gbps, a dedicated IPv4 and IPv6, and no published overage rate or fair-use threshold. There is no provider-side egress allowlist or no-internet switch in the VPS API; the firewall guide is iptables in the guest, and the Edge Network Firewall is inbound.

source.quote: Most of the rules outlined in this guide assume that your iptables is configured by default to DROP incoming traffic, and that you selectively authorize incoming traffic.

rows.scenario: The bundle includes 1 TB to 10 TB of transfer, overage is $0.09 to $0.17 a GB, and outbound traffic is otherwise unrestricted.
rows.note: Both directions count against the allowance, but only outbound traffic over it is charged; allowances are halved in Mumbai, Sydney, Jakarta, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Sao Paulo. There is no outbound allowlist and no no-internet mode, and the instance's public IP (static if you attach one) is its egress address.

source.quote: Every Lightsail instance plan includes a data transfer allowance.

rows.scenario: The agent browses freely inside its plan allowance from a static IPv4, but an outbound allowlist has to be enforced inside the VM.
rows.note: Each plan includes 0.5–15 TB of egress, overage is $0.01/GB, and a VPC-only instance can be deployed with no public IP. Vultr Firewall filters only incoming traffic, so outbound allowlisting is UFW, iptables or firewalld on the instance. Outbound 25, 137–139 and 445 are blocked by default and can be removed by ticket.

source.quote: No, Vultr Firewall does not filter outgoing traffic from instances.

rows.scenario: 400 GB of dependencies costs nothing extra; Contabo reserves the right to throttle exceptional use.
rows.note: Inbound and outbound traffic are unmetered, with no per-GiB price and no allowance to exceed. The catch is a fair-use policy: Contabo may throttle exceptionally high or disruptive usage, the port is 200 Mbit/s on Cloud VPS 4, and the Terms do not guarantee the bandwidth actually available. Outbound firewall rules are not offered.

source.quote: Outgoing Traffic: Unlimited — fair usage policy applies based on average server workloads.

rows.scenario: Model responses and logs fit inside the 4 TB that comes with the Linode 4 GB; beyond the allowance, transfer costs $0.005 a GB.
rows.note: Outbound transfer is pooled per account and prorated for part-months; inbound and intra-datacentre traffic is free. G8 and GPU plans include no transfer. Cloud Firewall outbound rules can restrict destinations, or drop everything.

source.quote: Metered outbound network transfer (egress) that includes 1 TB - 20 TB of prorated network transfer allowance

scenario.title: The agent downloads 400 GB of dependencies
scenario.setup: A build agent pulls container images and model weights all day. The job works everywhere; the bill and the controls do not.

beats.what: Outbound is open by default at most providers, so the download starts without configuration.
The provider either bills per GB, includes an allowance, or publishes nothing at all.
You try to narrow the agent to a package registry and find out whether the rule is enforced outside the machine.

scenario.turn: At $0.02 or $0.15 a gigabyte, 400 GB is a line item; at Boat, Sandboxer and Sprites it is free. The second half is control: a proxy the agent can bypass is not a network boundary.

questions: Is the default open or closed, and does a deny-all rule also block DNS?
Is the allowlist enforced outside the machine, or by a proxy the agent can bypass with a raw socket?
Is there a static egress IP, what does it cost, and is it per sandbox or per account?
Is egress free, metered, or unpublished — and what is the allowance before overage?
Can sandboxes reach each other over a private network, or does everything go out to the internet?
